lessons.t: Finding the question before the numbers
lessons.intro: You will learn to find the single question a problem is asking before you touch any numbers. This stops you doing arithmetic that never answers what was asked.

cards.b: The question is usually the last sentence, or the phrase starting with how many, how much or what is. Find it first and hold it in your mind while you read.
Answers have a form, such as a count, a time, a price or a fraction. Knowing which one you need tells you which numbers matter.
The first read gives you the story and the second gives you the facts. Most errors come from calculating after only a quick skim.

fig.title: Reading routine
fig.note: Do the first two steps before any sum.

ex.q: In the problem 'Ben has 14 apples and gives 6 to Cara. How many apples does Ben have left?', what is the unknown?
ex.why: The final sentence asks how many apples Ben has left, so that is the unknown. Cara and the 6 apples are facts used along the way, not the answer.

lessons.tip: Circle the question before you pick up a calculator.

quiz.q: Which phrase usually signals the question in a word problem?
quiz.why: How many, how much and what is are the phrases that ask for the unknown.

quiz.q: In 'A shop has 40 pens and sells 15, how many are left?', what is the unknown?
quiz.why: The question asks how many are left, so pens left is the unknown.

lessons.intro: You will learn to separate the numbers that change the answer from the background details in a problem. Using only the useful numbers keeps your working short and accurate.

cards.b: Some numbers describe the situation while others are simply background. Only the numbers that change the result belong in your working.
Numbers attached to a count, a rate or a price are usually the ones you need. A colour, a name or a year rarely changes the calculation.
Tick the numbers you use and cross out the ones you do not. A quick mark on the page stops an irrelevant figure creeping into your sum.

fig.title: Which numbers feed the egg count
fig.note: Only the laying hens feed the egg count.

ex.q: A class has 18 children. 6 are absent. Each child present gets 2 stickers. How many stickers are given out?
ex.why: Only the 12 children present get stickers, since 18 minus 6 is 12. Then 12 times 2 gives 24.

lessons.tip: If a number does not change the answer, it is a distractor.

quiz.q: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. The label says it is red. What is its area?
quiz.why: Area is length times width, 8 times 5, and the colour is not needed.

quiz.q: A farmer has 12 hens and 3 cows. 4 hens lay one egg each per day. How many eggs per day?
quiz.why: Only the 4 hens that lay eggs count, and each lays one, so the total is 4.

lessons.t: Naming the unknown with a letter
lessons.intro: You will learn to give the unknown a letter, such as n, so you can write the problem as a short statement. This turns a story into an equation you can solve.

cards.h: Choose a letter for the unknown
cards.b: Pick a letter that reminds you of the thing, such as c for cost or n for number. Say what it stands for before writing anything else.
Turn each fact into a line that includes the letter. If a box holds 4 pens and you have n boxes, the total number of pens is 4n.
Undo the operations one at a time, doing the same thing to both sides so the equation stays balanced. Then check that your answer fits the story.

fig.title: Naming a pattern with n
fig.note: Each term is 3 more than the last, starting from n.

ex.q: A box holds 4 pens. Ali has some boxes and 20 pens in total. How many boxes does Ali have?
ex.why: Let n be the number of boxes, so 4n equals 20. Dividing both sides by 4 gives n equals 5.

lessons.tip: Write down what your letter stands for before you write any equation.

quiz.q: If c is the cost of one ticket and 3 tickets cost 27 pounds, what is c?
quiz.why: Dividing 27 by 3 gives 9, so one ticket costs 9 pounds.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly uses n for 'a number increased by 5 is 12'?
quiz.why: Increased by 5 means add 5, so n plus 5 equals 12.

lessons.intro: You will learn which everyday words mean add, subtract, multiply or divide. Knowing these words lets you write the calculation before you worry about the numbers.

cards.b: Total, altogether, sum and in all signal addition. When two groups are joined, add their amounts to find the whole.
Left, difference, remain and fewer than point to subtraction. For fewer than, take the smaller number away from the larger, so 7 fewer than 20 is 20 minus 7.
Each, every and times usually mean multiply, while share equally and per can mean divide. Read the phrase carefully to tell which one applies.

fig.title: Common key words
fig.note: Fewer than reverses the order you subtract in.

ex.q: Jo has 3 bags, with 8 apples in each bag. Which calculation gives the total number of apples?
ex.why: Each bag holds 8 apples and there are 3 bags, so the total is 3 times 8, which is 24.

lessons.tip: The word each in a problem usually means multiply.

quiz.q: Which calculation matches '7 fewer than 20'?
quiz.why: Fewer than means take away, so 20 minus 7 gives 13.

quiz.q: Which word in a problem most often signals multiplication?
quiz.why: Each, when there are several equal groups, points to multiplying the group size by the number of groups.

lessons.t: Reading units and keeping them straight
lessons.intro: You will learn to spot units such as metres, minutes and pounds, and to make them match before you calculate. Mixed units are one of the most common causes of wrong answers.

cards.h: Units are part of the answer
cards.b: A number on its own is not enough. 5 means very little, but 5 km and 5 minutes describe very different quantities.
You cannot add 2 hours to 45 minutes directly. Change 2 hours into 120 minutes, then add to get 165 minutes.
Make sure your answer uses the unit the question asks for. If it asks for hours, convert your minutes back before you answer.

fig.title: Convert before you calculate
fig.note: Matching units comes before any arithmetic.

ex.q: A journey is 2 hours. Another is 45 minutes. What is their total time in minutes?
ex.why: Convert 2 hours into 120 minutes first. Adding 45 minutes gives 165 minutes.

lessons.tip: Write the unit next to every number as you go.

quiz.q: How many metres is 3.5 km?
quiz.why: One kilometre is 1000 metres, so 3.5 times 1000 is 3500.

quiz.q: A car travels 60 km in 1 hour at a steady speed. How far does it go in 30 minutes?
quiz.why: Half an hour is half the time, so the car covers half of 60 km, which is 30 km.

lessons.intro: You will learn to notice facts a problem assumes without stating them, such as a dozen being 12. Spotting these hidden facts lets you use all the information in a question.

cards.b: A dozen means 12, a pair means 2 and a century means 100 years. Writers often skip these because they expect you to know them.
A week has 7 days, an hour has 60 minutes and a right angle is 90 degrees. These facts can give you a missing number without any extra data.
Add each hidden fact to your list of givens as soon as you spot it. Keeping it visible stops you forgetting it when you reach the calculation.

fig.title: Hidden facts to remember
fig.note: These facts are often not stated in the question.

ex.q: A baker makes 4 dozen rolls and sells 30. How many rolls are left?
ex.why: 4 dozen is 4 times 12, which is 48. Taking away 30 leaves 18 rolls.

lessons.tip: Before you calculate, ask what common words in the problem secretly mean.

quiz.q: How many days are in 3 weeks?
quiz.why: Each week has 7 days, and 3 times 7 is 21.

quiz.q: A shop sells eggs in boxes of a dozen. How many eggs are in 5 boxes?
quiz.why: A dozen is 12, and 5 times 12 gives 60 eggs.

lessons.t: Sorting information into a quick table
lessons.intro: You will learn to list the facts from a problem in a simple table. A table shows at a glance what you know, what you need and what is still missing.

cards.b: Name the columns after what is being compared, such as item, number or price. Good headings make it obvious where each fact belongs.
Put every number from the question into the right cell, leaving a blank for the unknown. Blank cells show clearly what you still need to work out.
Once the table is full, you can often see which row or column to combine. The layout shows which calculation connects the facts.

fig.title: Pens and pads table
fig.note: Price is per item, in pounds.

ex.q: Pens cost 2 pounds each, with 4 bought. Pads cost 5 pounds each, with 3 bought. What is the total spent?
ex.why: Pens cost 4 times 2, which is 8. Pads cost 3 times 5, which is 15. Adding gives 23 pounds.

lessons.tip: Draw the table on scrap paper before writing any sums.

quiz.q: A table has columns Item, Quantity and Price each. Which two are multiplied to get a row's total?
quiz.why: The quantity times the price per item gives the total for that row.

quiz.q: 5 bags each hold 6 apples. What is the total number of apples?
quiz.why: Five bags of six is 5 times 6, which gives 30 apples.

lessons.intro: You will learn to tell which details in a problem you need and which are just noise. Dropping the right details keeps your working short and your answer correct.

cards.b: Problems often include a year, a name or an extra price that does not affect the answer. Ask whether each number changes the result.
Imagine the question without that detail. If the question still makes sense and the answer would be unchanged, the detail is extra.
A number that looks irrelevant can be the key to a hidden fact, such as a rate or a unit. Only discard it after you have checked.

fig.title: Needed versus extra
fig.note: Check each number before you drop it.

ex.q: A train has 240 seats and leaves at 9:00. 180 seats are sold and the fare is 15 pounds. How many seats are free?
ex.why: The time and fare do not change the seat count. 240 minus 180 leaves 60 free seats.

lessons.tip: If a number does not change the answer, it is a distractor.

quiz.q: A book has 320 pages and a red cover. You read 40 pages a day. How many days to finish?
quiz.why: The colour is irrelevant, and 320 pages divided by 40 pages a day gives 8 days.

quiz.q: A shop has 12 shirts at 20 pounds each, and it opened in 1998. What is the stock value?
quiz.why: The opening year does not affect the value, and 12 shirts at 20 pounds each is 240 pounds.

lessons.t: Checking whether an answer makes sense
lessons.intro: You will learn to estimate a sensible answer before you calculate, and to judge whether your final answer is plausible. A quick check catches many slips.

cards.b: Replace numbers with easy nearby values, such as 19 with 20. The rough answer shows the size of result you should expect.
If your estimate is about 80 and your exact answer is 7600, something has gone wrong. Answers far from the estimate usually signal a misplaced decimal point or a missing step.

cards.h: Ask if the size is possible
cards.b: A shopping total cannot be negative, and a person cannot walk 500 km in an hour. Asking whether the answer is possible is a quick sanity test.

fig.title: Estimate versus exact
fig.note: Rounding gives a close, quick check of 48 times 21.

ex.q: Ben buys 4 tickets at 19 pounds each. Which total is sensible?
ex.why: Rounding 19 to 20 gives 4 times 20, about 80. The exact answer 76 is close, while the other options are far off in size.

lessons.tip: Estimate first so you know roughly what size of answer to expect.

quiz.q: Which is the best quick estimate of 48 times 21?
quiz.why: Rounding gives about 50 times 20, which is about 1000, close to the exact 1008.

quiz.q: What is a sensible cost for 5 bags, each costing 3 pounds?
quiz.why: 5 times 3 is 15, so 15 pounds is right and the others are the wrong size.

lessons.t: Restating a word problem in one line
lessons.intro: You will learn to restate a word problem as one short equation. Writing the problem in one line makes clear what to calculate and what you are trying to find.

cards.b: Cross out words that carry no numbers or relationships. What remains is the core of the problem, often one or two short phrases.
Use a letter for the unknown and link the facts with operations. For example, 3 boxes of 8 plus 5 loose items is 3 times 8 plus 5.
Work out the one line using the usual order of operations. Then reread the question to be sure your number answers exactly what was asked.

fig.title: From story to sentence
fig.note: The one-line version is what you calculate.

ex.q: A cinema has 3 rows of 12 seats and 6 extra seats. How many seats in total?
ex.why: Write it as 3 times 12 plus 6. Multiplying first gives 36, then adding 6 gives 42.

lessons.tip: Write the problem as one line before you pick a calculation.

quiz.q: Which single line best restates 'Each of 5 boxes holds 7 cards, and 4 cards are removed'?
quiz.why: There are 5 boxes of 7 cards, giving 5 times 7, then 4 cards are removed by subtracting 4.

quiz.q: What is the value of 2 + 3 times 4?
quiz.why: Multiplication comes first, so 3 times 4 gives 12, then adding 2 gives 14.

lessons.intro: You will learn what a ratio tells you about the relationship between two quantities. A ratio says how many of one thing there are for each of another.

cards.b: A ratio of 3 to 2 means for every 3 parts of one thing there are 2 parts of another. It does not tell you the total number of items.
To find the total, add the parts. A 3 to 2 ratio of red to blue paint has 5 parts altogether.

cards.h: Each part has a real size
cards.b: Parts are equal groups, so 3 parts might be 3 litres and 2 parts 2 litres. Multiply the part size by each number in the ratio to get real amounts.

fig.title: Red to blue paint parts
fig.note: That is 3 parts red to 2 parts blue.

ex.q: The ratio of boys to girls is 2:3. There are 15 students in total. How many are girls?
ex.why: The parts total 2 plus 3, which is 5. Each part is 15 divided by 5, which is 3, so 3 girls' parts make 9 girls.

lessons.tip: A ratio counts parts, not people, until you scale it.

quiz.q: In the ratio 4 to 1, how many parts are there in total?
quiz.why: Adding 4 and 1 gives 5 equal parts altogether.

quiz.q: A class has ratio 3:5 of girls to boys. What fraction of the class are girls?
quiz.why: The parts total 8, and the girls are 3 of those 8 parts, so the fraction is 3/8.

lessons.t: Scaling a recipe up and down
lessons.intro: You will learn to scale a recipe or mixture by multiplying every quantity by the same factor. Scaling correctly keeps the taste and balance the same.

cards.b: Divide the new number of servings by the old number. Going from 4 servings to 6 gives a factor of 1.5, so every amount is multiplied by 1.5.
Apply the same factor to each quantity, not just to some of them. Missing one ingredient changes the balance of the whole recipe.
To make half a recipe, multiply every amount by one half. A recipe using 300 g of flour for 6 people becomes 150 g for 3 people.

fig.title: Scaling a recipe by 2
fig.note: Every ingredient doubles when servings double.

ex.q: A recipe for 4 people needs 250 g of rice. How much rice for 6 people?
ex.why: Six people divided by four people gives a factor of 1.5. Multiplying 250 g by 1.5 gives 375 g.

lessons.tip: Work out the scale factor first, then apply it to every line.

quiz.q: A cake recipe for 8 uses 200 ml of milk. How much milk for 4 people?
quiz.why: Four is half of eight, so the milk is halved to 100 ml.

quiz.q: A recipe for 2 people needs 3 eggs. How many eggs for 8 people?
quiz.why: Eight is four times two, so 3 eggs times 4 gives 12 eggs.

lessons.intro: You will learn to find a unit rate, the amount for one unit, by dividing a total by its number of units. Unit rates let you compare differently sized amounts fairly.

cards.h: A unit rate is per one
cards.b: A unit rate is the quantity for exactly one unit, such as pounds per kilogram or miles per hour. It is the basis for almost every rate problem.
To find the unit rate, divide the total amount by the number of units. Five litres shared across 2 bottles is 2.5 litres per bottle.
Once you know the rate, multiply it by any new number of units. If one bottle holds 2.5 litres, then 6 bottles hold 15 litres.

fig.title: Cost of 1 to 4 pens (pounds)
fig.note: Each extra pen adds 3 pounds, so the unit rate is 3.

ex.q: A 6-pack of juice costs 9 pounds. What does one carton cost?
ex.why: Divide the total of 9 pounds by 6 cartons, which gives 1.5 pounds per carton.

lessons.tip: Always divide the total by the count to find the rate for one.

quiz.q: A car drives 180 miles on 6 gallons of fuel. How many miles per gallon?
quiz.why: Dividing 180 miles by 6 gallons gives 30 miles per gallon.

quiz.q: Which is cheaper per gram: 500 g for 2 pounds, or 750 g for 2.7 pounds?
quiz.why: 2 pounds over 500 g is 0.004 per gram, while 2.7 pounds over 750 g is 0.0036 per gram, so the 750 g pack is cheaper.

lessons.intro: You will learn to compare package sizes by working out the price per unit. This shows which option gives better value for money.

cards.b: A large pack may cost more in total yet less per gram. You need the unit price to know which pack gives more for each pound.
Convert both prices to the same unit, such as per 100 g or per litre. Make sure the units match before comparing the numbers.
The smaller unit price is the better value, provided the products are similar in quality. Compare the unit price, not the size of the box.

fig.title: Pence per 100 g
fig.note: The lower pence per 100 g is the better value.

ex.q: Pack A is 500 g for 3 pounds. Pack B is 750 g for 4 pounds. Which pack gives better value?
ex.why: Pack A costs 3 divided by 500, about 0.006 per gram. Pack B costs 4 divided by 750, about 0.0053 per gram, which is lower.

lessons.tip: Divide price by quantity and compare the results on the same unit.

quiz.q: Pack X is 2 litres for 5 pounds. Pack Y is 3 litres for 8 pounds. Which is better per litre?
quiz.why: Pack X is 5 divided by 2, which is 2.50, while Pack Y is 8 divided by 3, about 2.67, so X is cheaper.

quiz.q: A 4-pack costs 6 pounds and a 6-pack costs 8 pounds. Which pack is cheaper per item?
quiz.why: The 4-pack is 1.50 each and the 6-pack is about 1.33 each, so the 6-pack is cheaper per item.

lessons.intro: You will learn how speed, distance and time connect, so you can find any one of them when you know the other two. These problems appear in everyday travel and in many test questions.

cards.b: If you travel at 50 miles per hour for 3 hours, you cover 150 miles. Speed tells you how fast, time tells you how long, and distance is the result.
To find time, divide distance by speed. To find speed, divide distance by time. Keep the units consistent, such as miles with hours.
Convert minutes into hours before using speed in miles per hour. 90 minutes is 1.5 hours, so at 60 miles per hour you cover 90 miles.

fig.title: Speed, time and distance
fig.note: Distance is speed multiplied by time.

ex.q: A cyclist rides 36 km at 12 km/h. How long does the ride take?
ex.why: Time equals distance divided by speed, so 36 km divided by 12 km/h gives 3 hours.

lessons.tip: Check the units match before you divide, since minutes and hours cannot be mixed.

quiz.q: A train goes 240 km in 4 hours. What is its speed?
quiz.why: Speed equals distance divided by time, so 240 divided by 4 gives 60 km/h.

quiz.q: A runner covers 2 km in 10 minutes. What is the speed in km per hour?
quiz.why: 10 minutes is one sixth of an hour, so 2 divided by one sixth gives 12 km/h.

lessons.intro: You will learn to read percentages as parts out of 100 and turn them into fractions or decimals. This makes discounts, taxes and tips quick to work out.

cards.b: 25 percent means 25 out of every 100, which is one quarter. Writing it as 0.25 lets you multiply directly.
Convert the percentage to a decimal, then multiply. To find 15 percent of 80, multiply 80 by 0.15 to get 12.
To find what is left after a discount, subtract the percentage from 100. After 20 percent off, you pay 80 percent of the price.

fig.title: A 20 percent discount
fig.note: After 20 percent off, you pay 80 percent of the price.

ex.q: A jacket costs 60 pounds and is reduced by 25 percent. What is the new price?
ex.why: A 25 percent discount leaves 75 percent, so 60 times 0.75 gives 45 pounds.

lessons.tip: To find 10 percent, move the decimal point one place to the left.

quiz.q: What is 30 percent of 200?
quiz.why: 30 percent is 0.3, and 0.3 times 200 equals 60.

quiz.q: A bill of 40 pounds has 10 percent added. What is the total?
quiz.why: 10 percent of 40 is 4, so adding it gives 44 pounds.

lessons.intro: You will learn to solve proportions, where two ratios are equal and one value is missing. Cross-multiplying gives you a quick way to find the missing number.

cards.b: A proportion says two fractions are equal, such as 2 over 3 equal to 4 over 6. Put the known values in matching positions.
Multiply the top of each fraction by the bottom of the other, and set the results equal. For x over 5 equal to 4.5 over 3, 3x equals 22.5, so x is 7.5.
Substitute your answer back into both ratios and see whether they match. Make sure the answer is a sensible size for the situation.

fig.title: Equal ratios in a table
fig.note: Each column keeps the same ratio of cups to eggs.

ex.q: If 3 pens cost 4.50 pounds, how much do 5 pens cost?
ex.why: The pens and cost are in proportion, so x over 5 equals 4.50 over 3. Cross-multiplying gives 3x equals 22.5, so x is 7.5 pounds.

lessons.tip: Cross-multiplying works whenever two fractions are equal.

quiz.q: Solve x over 4 equals 9 over 12.
quiz.why: Cross-multiplying gives 12x equals 36, so x equals 3.

quiz.q: If 2 kg of apples cost 5 pounds, what do 6 kg cost?
quiz.why: Six kilograms is three times 2 kg, so the cost is 3 times 5, which is 15 pounds.

lessons.t: Splitting a total in a given ratio
lessons.intro: You will learn to split a total amount into parts in a given ratio, such as sharing money or mixing paint. The same method works for any number of parts.

cards.b: Add all the numbers in the ratio to find how many equal parts the whole is split into. A ratio of 2:3:5 has 10 parts in total.
Divide the total amount by the number of parts. If 500 ml is shared in ratio 2:3, that is 5 parts, so each part is 100 ml.
Multiply the value of one part by each number in the ratio. The shares for 2:3 from 500 ml are 200 ml and 300 ml.

fig.title: Splitting in a ratio
fig.note: Each share is one part times its ratio number.

ex.q: 90 pounds is shared between Ann and Ben in ratio 2:1. How much does Ann get?
ex.why: The total is 3 parts, so one part is 90 divided by 3, which is 30. Ann gets 2 parts, which is 60 pounds.

lessons.tip: Check that your shares add back up to the original total.

quiz.q: A 20 litre mix is in ratio 3:2 of blue to white. How many litres of blue are there?
quiz.why: There are 5 parts in total, so each part is 4 litres, and blue is 3 parts, which is 12 litres.

quiz.q: Three friends share 60 sweets in ratio 1:2:3. How many does the middle friend get?
quiz.why: There are 6 parts, so one part is 10 sweets, and the middle friend has 2 parts, which is 20 sweets.

lessons.intro: You will learn to change a rate from one pair of units to another, such as kilometres per hour into metres per second. Getting the units right keeps travel and physics problems correct.

cards.b: A rate has two units, so convert each one. Kilometres to metres multiplies by 1000, and hours to seconds divides by 3600.
Multiply by a fraction equal to one, such as 1000 metres over 1 kilometre. The unwanted units cancel out, leaving the ones you need.
Divide the km per hour value by 3.6 to get metres per second. So 36 km/h becomes 10 m/s, since 36 divided by 3.6 is 10.

fig.title: Speed conversions
fig.note: Divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s.

ex.q: A car travels at 90 km/h. What is its speed in m/s?
ex.why: Divide 90 by 3.6 to convert km per hour to m per second, which gives 25 m/s.

lessons.tip: Dividing km/h by 3.6 gives m/s, a conversion worth memorising.

quiz.q: A cyclist rides at 18 km/h. What is that in m/s?
quiz.why: Divide 18 by 3.6 to get 5 metres per second.

quiz.q: How many seconds are in 2 hours?
quiz.why: One hour has 3600 seconds, so two hours have 7200 seconds.

lessons.intro: You will learn to combine work rates when two people or machines do a job together. Adding rates per hour shows how long the job takes with both working.

cards.b: A worker who finishes a job in 6 hours does one sixth of it each hour. Write each rate as a fraction of the whole job per hour.
Add the hourly fractions to get the combined rate. One sixth plus one third is one half, so together they finish half the job each hour.
Take the reciprocal of the combined rate to find the time. A rate of one half per hour means the job takes 2 hours.

fig.title: Hours to finish a job alone
fig.note: Together they finish faster than either one alone.

ex.q: Tom takes 4 hours to paint a wall alone, and Sara also takes 4 hours. How long together?
ex.why: Each person does one quarter of the wall per hour, so together they do one half per hour. The wall takes 2 hours.

lessons.tip: Combine rates per hour, never add the times directly.

quiz.q: A pump fills a tank in 3 hours and another pump fills the same tank in 6 hours. How long together?
quiz.why: The rates are one third and one sixth per hour, which add to one half, so the time is 2 hours.

quiz.q: Machine A makes a part in 10 minutes and machine B also takes 10 minutes. How many parts per hour together?
quiz.why: Each machine makes 6 parts an hour, so together they make 12 parts an hour.

lessons.t: Breaking a problem into ordered steps
lessons.intro: You will learn to split a multi-step problem into smaller stages and solve them in the right order. Clear stages stop you trying to do everything at once.

cards.b: Start from what the question asks for, then work out which intermediate values you need to reach it. This keeps your plan focused.
Find each intermediate result and write it down with its unit. Each stage's answer becomes a given for the next stage.
List the stages in the order they depend on each other. Some stages cannot start until another has finished, so sequence matters.

fig.title: Stages that feed each other
fig.note: Each stage's answer feeds the next.

ex.q: A shop sells pens at 3 pounds each. Ali buys 4 pens and pays with a 20 pound note. How much change does he get?
ex.why: First find the cost, 4 times 3, which is 12 pounds. Then subtract that from the 20 pound note to get 8 pounds change.

lessons.tip: Name each stage with a short label before you calculate it.

quiz.q: Which stage must come first when finding the average speed of a trip?
quiz.why: You need the total distance and total time before you can divide to find the average speed.

quiz.q: A problem needs the cost of 5 items, then a 10 percent discount on that cost. Which step comes first?
quiz.why: The discount needs the cost to be known first, so the cost of 5 items comes before the discount.

lessons.intro: You will learn to record each intermediate result clearly so you can follow a multi-step calculation without losing track. Writing values down prevents the errors that come from holding numbers in your head.

cards.b: Give each intermediate value a name and unit, such as cost after tax. A labelled value is easy to find when a later step needs it.
Carry the full value through the steps and round only at the end. Rounding early can shift your final answer by a noticeable amount.
Glance back at your labelled values to confirm each one follows from the last. A quick scan catches a number copied wrongly.

fig.title: Tracking each stage
fig.note: Write each result before you move on.

ex.q: Start with 8. Add 5. Then double the result. What is the final value?
ex.why: Start with 8, add 5 to get 13, then double it to get 26. Keeping the intermediate 13 labelled makes the final step clear.

lessons.tip: Write intermediate values on separate lines, never only in your head.

quiz.q: Why should you carry full decimals through a multi-step calculation?
o: Rounding early can change the final answer
quiz.why: Early rounding compounds small errors, so keep full precision until the end.

quiz.q: Start with 10, subtract 4, then multiply by 3. What is the result?
quiz.why: 10 minus 4 gives 6, and 6 times 3 gives 18.

lessons.intro: You will learn to find a starting value by undoing each operation in reverse order, beginning from the final answer. This is useful when a problem gives you the end result.

cards.b: Addition is undone by subtraction, and multiplication is undone by division. Apply the opposite of each step in the reverse sequence.
Write the final value, then undo the last operation first. Each reversal gives you the value that was there just before that step.
Once you have a starting value, apply the original steps forwards to confirm you return to the final answer. This catches reversal errors.

fig.title: Reverse the chain
fig.note: Undo the steps in the opposite order.

ex.q: A number is doubled, then 6 is added, giving 26. What was the number?
ex.why: Undo the addition first: 26 minus 6 is 20. Then undo the doubling: 20 divided by 2 is 10.

lessons.tip: Undo the last step first, then work your way back to the start.

quiz.q: A number is tripled and then 4 is subtracted, giving 11. What was the number?
quiz.why: Undo the subtraction, 11 plus 4 is 15, then undo the tripling, 15 divided by 3 gives 5.

quiz.q: Sam thinks of a number, adds 9, then halves the result to get 7. What was the number?
quiz.why: Undo the halving: 7 times 2 is 14. Then undo the addition: 14 minus 9 is 5.

lessons.intro: You will learn to apply several percentage changes one after another without the common mistake of adding percentages. Each change applies to the value left after the previous change.

cards.b: A 10 percent rise followed by a 10 percent fall does not return you to the start. The second change is taken from the increased value.
Turn each change into a multiplier, such as 1.1 for a 10 percent rise or 0.9 for a 10 percent fall. Multiply the starting value by each multiplier in turn.
A 20 percent rise followed by a 20 percent fall is not 0 percent overall. Calculate the result step by step rather than adding or subtracting percentages.

fig.title: Two 10 percent changes
fig.note: Two equal percent changes do not cancel out exactly.

ex.q: A price of 200 pounds rises 10 percent, then falls 10 percent. What is the final price?
ex.why: A 10 percent rise makes 220 pounds. A 10 percent fall from 220 is 198 pounds, not back to 200.

lessons.tip: Multiply by 1.1 then by 0.9 instead of adding and subtracting percentages.

quiz.q: A value of 50 rises 20 percent, then rises 20 percent again. What is the final value?
quiz.why: Each 20 percent rise multiplies by 1.2, so 50 times 1.2 times 1.2 gives 72.

quiz.q: Which is the multiplier for a 15 percent fall?
quiz.why: A 15 percent fall leaves 85 percent of the value, which is 0.85.

lessons.intro: You will learn the order in which to work out a calculation with brackets, multiplication, division, addition and subtraction. Doing the steps in the wrong order gives a confidently wrong answer.

cards.b: Work out anything inside brackets before doing anything outside them. In (2 plus 3) times 4, the 2 plus 3 is done first to give 5.
Multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction. So 2 plus 3 times 4 is 2 plus 12, which equals 14.

cards.h: Equal ranks go left to right
cards.b: Operations of the same rank, such as adding then subtracting, are done left to right. Multiplying and then dividing follows the same rule.

fig.title: Order of operations
fig.note: Multiply before adding, then add the result.

ex.q: What is 10 minus 2 times 3 plus 4?
ex.why: Multiply first, so 2 times 3 is 6, leaving 10 minus 6 plus 4. Working left to right gives 4 plus 4, which is 8.

lessons.tip: Brackets first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.

quiz.q: What is (7 + 3) times 2 minus 5?
quiz.why: Brackets give 10, then times 2 gives 20, and minus 5 gives 15.

quiz.q: What is 18 divided by 3 plus 2 times 4?
quiz.why: Division and multiplication come first, giving 6 plus 8, which equals 14.

lessons.intro: You will learn to work out change from the money handed over and the cost of the items bought. Doing this in clear steps prevents slips when several items are involved.

cards.b: Add up the price of everything bought, multiplying price by quantity for each item. Only then compare the total with the money handed over.
Change equals the amount handed over minus the total cost. Paying 50 pounds for 36.40 pounds of goods gives 13.60 pounds change.
Add the change to the total and confirm it equals the amount paid. This simple reverse check catches most subtraction errors.

fig.title: Paid and change
fig.note: Change is what you get back from the amount paid.

ex.q: You buy 3 books at 7.50 pounds each and 1 pen at 2.25 pounds, paying with 30 pounds. What change do you get?
ex.why: Three books cost 22.50 pounds and the pen costs 2.25, so the total is 24.75. Then 30 minus 24.75 gives 5.25 pounds change.

lessons.tip: Check by adding the change back onto the total to reach the amount paid.

quiz.q: You pay 20 pounds for items costing 13.80 pounds. What is the change?
quiz.why: Subtract the cost from the amount paid: 20 minus 13.80 leaves 6.20 pounds.

quiz.q: Two shirts cost 12.50 pounds each and you pay with 30 pounds. How much change?
quiz.why: Two shirts cost 25 pounds in total, and 30 minus 25 leaves 5 pounds change.

lessons.t: Tracking a running total over days
lessons.intro: You will learn to track a running total when amounts are added or removed day by day. A running table makes it clear what the total is at any point.

cards.b: Begin with the amount you already have on day one. Every later total depends on this starting figure.
Carry the total forward by applying each day's change to the previous total. A day that adds 15 turns a total of 25 into 40.
If the daily change rises steadily, the total follows a predictable pattern. Spotting the pattern lets you predict later totals without listing every day.

fig.title: Running savings total
fig.note: Savings grow by 5 more each day than the day before.

ex.q: A jar has 4 coins. Each day 3 are added and 2 are removed. How many coins are there after 3 days?
ex.why: Each day the net change is plus 3 minus 2, which is plus 1. Starting at 4, three days of plus 1 give 7 coins.

lessons.tip: Track the net change per day, then multiply by the number of days when it stays constant.

quiz.q: A balance starts at 100 and loses 15 each week. What is it after 3 weeks?
quiz.why: Three weeks of losing 15 takes away 45, leaving 55.

quiz.q: Savings: day 1 is 10, day 2 adds 15, and day 3 adds 20. What is the total after day 3?
quiz.why: Add each day's amount to the running total: 10, then 25, then 45.

lessons.intro: You will learn to find fractions of quantities and combine them within multi-step problems. Working with fractions carefully keeps each stage of the calculation accurate.

cards.h: Find a fraction of a quantity
cards.b: Divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top number. Three quarters of 20 is 20 divided by 4, times 3, which equals 15.
When a fraction is taken away, the amount left is the rest of the whole. If you spend one third of 30 pounds, you have two thirds left, which is 20 pounds.
Before adding or comparing fractions, rewrite them with the same denominator. A half plus a third becomes three sixths plus two sixths, which is five sixths.

fig.title: Fractions and decimals
fig.note: Fractions and decimals describe the same share.

ex.q: A tank holds 60 litres. A quarter is used on Monday, then a third of what is left is used on Tuesday. How much is left?
ex.why: A quarter of 60 is 15, leaving 45. A third of 45 is 15 used, so 30 litres remain.

lessons.tip: Find what remains after each fraction before taking the next one.

quiz.q: What is 3/4 of 20?
quiz.why: 20 divided by 4 is 5, and 3 times 5 gives 15.

quiz.q: What is 1/2 plus 1/3?
quiz.why: Write them as three sixths and two sixths, which add to five sixths.

lessons.t: Checking each step with a reverse check
lessons.intro: You will learn to test your answer by putting it back into the original problem, catching mistakes before you submit. A reverse check takes seconds and often reveals a slip.

cards.b: Put your final answer into the original question and see whether the facts still hold. If 60 comes from 12 boxes of 5, the check should confirm it.
To check a division, multiply the answer by the divisor and see whether you return to the original number. To check subtraction, add back.
If the check does not match, your answer is wrong somewhere, not the check. Go back through the steps and find where the values diverge.

fig.title: The check loop
fig.note: Repair any step where the check fails.

ex.q: A student says x = 5 solves 3x + 4 = 19. Which statement is correct?
ex.why: Substitute 5: 3 times 5 is 15, plus 4 gives 19, which matches the right side, so x equals 5 works.

lessons.tip: A quick check after the final line is worth more than a faster wrong answer.

quiz.q: A student divides 84 by 4 and gets 19. How can a reverse check reveal this?
quiz.why: Multiplying 19 by 4 gives 76, not 84, so the division was wrong.

quiz.q: Which operation undoes addition when you check an answer?
quiz.why: Subtraction reverses addition, so subtracting back should return the original starting value.

lessons.t: Solving a full multi-stage budget problem
lessons.intro: You will learn to combine ratio, rate, percentage and change steps in a single budget problem. Working through the stages in order gives you a complete answer you can check.

cards.b: List the income, fixed costs, variable costs and any percentages before calculating. This turns a long story into a clear sequence of smaller problems.
Name each intermediate figure, such as rent or savings, and use it in the next stage. Labels make it easy to spot where an error entered.
Confirm the parts add back to the whole and the final figure makes sense for the situation. A negative remainder signals a mistake somewhere.

fig.title: Monthly budget breakdown
fig.note: Income minus rent and food leaves 350 pounds.

ex.q: Income is 1200 pounds. Rent is 40 percent of income. Food costs 250 pounds. How much is left?
ex.why: 40 percent of 1200 is 480 for rent. 1200 minus 480 leaves 720, and minus 250 for food leaves 470 pounds.

lessons.tip: Check that all your spending and savings add up to your income.

quiz.q: A budget has 2000 pounds. 15 percent goes to savings, then 300 pounds goes on bills. How much is left?
quiz.why: 15 percent of 2000 is 300 for savings. Subtracting 300 and then 300 more leaves 1400 pounds.

quiz.q: A worker earns 12 pounds per hour and works 35 hours. What is the gross weekly pay?
quiz.why: Hours times rate gives 35 times 12, which is 420 pounds.
